turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

This is a tough one, yaar. Respect for Suresh-ji runs deep in the team, and now you’re the one who has to draw the line. That word “handle” from your director basically means the company has already decided the outcome—they just want you to execute it cleanly.

The hardest part isn’t the performance issue. It’s that you have to be the one to tell a 56-year-old man who’s given nearly two decades that his work is no longer good enough. That conversation carries a weight that goes beyond the org chart.

How are you feeling about it right now—more angry, more sad, or just dreading the actual meeting?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

This is the part that actually hurts the most, isn't it? The chai, the midnight fix, the way he claimed you as family in front of your mom... those aren't just nice stories. They're the reason this feels like a betrayal even though you're the one being asked to do it.

You're not just delivering metrics. You're breaking a relationship that made you feel safe when you were still figuring everything out. That's a different kind of loss.

How are you holding up with that weight right now?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

Yes. The books are right on this one. Direct, with the data, no dancing around it — that's the respectful way. But you're allowed to bring the humanity too. You can be clear *and* still the person he brought chai for.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

There's no version where you're not carrying some of the blame in his eyes, or in your own. That's the part that sucks. Letting him coast would just make you the villain to the rest of the team and to yourself later. The direct route at least keeps your integrity intact, even if it costs the relationship. You're not easing him out with good manners — you're doing the job no one else wants to do.
